newsitem.title: UK: Europe to follow Britain's buyback lead - JP Morgan.
newsitem.headline: Europe to follow Britain's buyback lead - JP Morgan.

text.p: Continental European companies are likely to follow their British counterparts in using share buy-backs to return excess cash to shareholders, U.S. investment bank JP Morgan said in a report released on Monday.
"This is something Europe can look forward to once the legislative environment changes," Gary Dugan, one of the authors of the report, told Reuters in an interview.

JP Morgan's report came in the wake of an announcement on Monday from a leading official at the German Justice Ministery saying that German companies ought in future be allowed to repurchase a maximum of 10 percent of their own equity.

Rainer Funke, state secretary of the German Justice Ministry, said the government would frame a new share law on an European Union directive which sets an upper limit of 10 percent for equity buybacks.
Share repurchases are, as a general rule, treated as a distribution by tax authorities in continental Europe and they are therefore subject to income tax, JP Morgan's report said.
But Dugan believes there are signs of change, although the process may be taking longer than expected.
JP Morgan had expected alterations to the rules in Germany, Switzerland and Sweden to take place ahead of other countries.

The three are still seen as the most likely candidates for change but Dugan said he now believed changes in Germany would not come in the next 12 months as they would be wrapped into more general changes in the tax system there.

Dugan said he understood that the French government was also in the process of reviewing the rules on taxation of share buy-backs, adding that a change could lead to moves by companies such as Elf, Renault, Peugeot and Carrefour.
The report says Swiss industrial companies "are in general cash rich and would appear to be very good candidates for share buybacks, given their high cost of equity".
It said that with short term rates of 2.2 percent and a cost of equity of 13.1 percent "there is obvious economic benefit in reducing cash balances and buying back shares".
Pharmaceuticals companies are highlighted as the most likely candidates for buy-backs in Switzerland, while in Germany Preussag, RWE, VEBA, BASF, Hoechst and Bayer are possibilities.

"In the case of the (German) chemicals sector, we expect compound dividend growth of seven percent over the next two years, which would equate to a cost of equity of about 10 percent. Hence retiring equity would appear to make economic sense for this sector," the report adds.
In Sweden, there is also substantial scope for buy-backs as the cost of equity "for many of the major companies" is well above both the cost of long-term debt and short-term interest rates, it said.

The report says recent studies of European share buy-backs showed that "repurchase programmes significantly increase shareholder value" and that "virtually all of the share price gain is achieved in the 60 days after the announcement, rather than the actual execution (of the programmes)".
This means firms should begin buying in shares at the time or soon after the announcement of plans "rather than waiting for several months as has generally been the case to date".
